bp: Modern web platforms do not merely display pages. They decide which posts rise, which products are recommended, which ads are sold, and which content is removed or demoted. Those decisions are increasingly made by AI systems, but the public record around them is often thin. A user, auditor, regulator, or affected business may want to know which model version made a decision, what provenance claims were attached to the data, and whether the platform can later change the story without being noticed. This paper serves that need by treating transparency as part of the web's operating machinery rather than as a voluntary report. Its real object is an audit trail for AI-mediated web decisions. The proposed Decentralised Trust Layer records provenance anchors, signed model metadata, and privacy-preserving inference receipts in an append-only transparency log, so later verification does not depend only on trusting the platform's memory or public relations statement.
wh: The hard part is that AI transparency pulls in opposite directions. Auditors need evidence detailed enough to check whether a platform ran the claimed model, followed the claimed data lineage, and produced receipts for actual decisions. Platforms, users, and laws also need privacy and trade-secret protection, so the evidence cannot simply expose every input, model detail, or user interaction. A second difficulty is tampering over time. A platform can publish a model card or policy document, but that document alone does not prove which model actually served a request last week or whether a record was quietly rewritten. A third difficulty is web scale: ranking, recommendation, advertising, and moderation happen per request, so any audit mechanism that adds heavy delay is unlikely to be deployed. The paper's tension is therefore verification versus secrecy, and public accountability versus per-request cost. It must make checking possible without turning every decision into a slow public leak.
naive: A smart beginner might ask each platform to keep internal logs and publish periodic transparency reports. That helps with narrative accountability, but it leaves the central proof problem unresolved: outsiders still have to trust that the log was complete, unchanged, and tied to the model that actually ran. Another beginner might require full disclosure of model internals and training data. That would make some checks easier, but it would expose private user information, proprietary systems, and security-sensitive details. A third simple path is manual audits on a small sample. That can catch some failures, but it does not create a routine receipt for ordinary AI decisions. The paper needs a mechanism that makes the trail hard to rewrite while keeping the sensitive contents controlled.
ap: The core idea is to give web AI decisions a public-verifiable paper trail without making the whole decision public. DTL does this by separating claims from secrets. A provenance claim says something about where data or a model came from; the system anchors that claim so later parties can check whether the same claim was present at the time. A model lineage registry binds a deployed model version to signed metadata, making model changes traceable instead of invisible. Inference transparency produces a receipt for a served decision while preserving privacy, so the receipt can prove that an accountable event occurred without spilling the full request. These records are placed in an append-only transparency log inspired by certificate transparency, the web security idea that certificates become harder to fake when they must appear in a public log. Decentralised audit sampling then lets outside checkers inspect pieces of the trail instead of trusting one owner.
mech: The mechanism starts before an AI decision is served. The platform prepares provenance statements about data and model artifacts, then anchors those statements in a form that can later be compared against the public record. It also registers model lineage: a particular deployed model version is bound to signed metadata, so a verifier can ask whether the version claimed for a decision matches a committed entry. When the platform handles a ranking, recommendation, advertising, or moderation request, it produces an inference receipt. The abstract says the receipt is privacy-preserving, so the receipt is not meant to dump the full user input or private model contents; it is a checkable trace that an inference happened under a claimed model and metadata state. The receipt or its commitment is added to an append-only transparency log, where new entries extend the log rather than replacing old ones. Later, an auditor samples the log, verifies signatures and proof material, checks that receipt generation and proof verification are consistent with the protocol, and looks for missing or contradictory records. The paper's evaluation focuses on the measurable plumbing: cryptographic overhead, logging overhead, proof verification cost, per-request receipt cost, and proof size. The reported shape is microsecond-scale receipt generation and logarithmic proof sizes, meaning the proof grows slowly as the log grows.
math: The main mathematical idea is commitment over time. A cryptographic commitment is like sealing a claim in a tamper-evident envelope: later, the holder can show that the claim matches the envelope, but changing the claim should be detectable. Hashing supplies the usual building block. It turns a record into a short fingerprint; if the record changes, the fingerprint should change in a way that is infeasible to fake. An append-only transparency log adds a second idea: ordered accumulation. Instead of storing isolated receipts, the system stores a growing sequence whose current state can prove that earlier entries are still included. Logarithmic proof size means checking membership or consistency needs evidence that grows with the height of the log structure, not with every entry one by one. Digital signatures add accountability by tying metadata to an authorized signer. Privacy-preserving receipts add constrained disclosure: reveal enough structure to verify that the event followed the protocol, but not enough to reconstruct private inputs or proprietary details. Decentralised audit sampling uses probability in a plain way: auditors cannot inspect every request, so sampled checks are meant to make cheating risky by increasing the chance that omissions or contradictions are noticed. The tradeoff is public verifiability versus privacy, and audit coverage versus operating cost.
dots: This paper sits between several recurring repo families. It belongs with Privacy, Federated & Security because it asks what useful evidence may cross a boundary while sensitive data remains hidden. It also belongs with Misinformation & Trust because trust is treated as a chain: source, model version, inference event, log entry, and later verification. The surface system is web AI, but the affected decisions are the same ones studied across ranking, recommendation, advertising, and moderation papers: platforms sort a huge pile of possible content or ads and show only a few. DTL does not improve the ranker itself; it makes the decision trail inspectable. It is also near responsible-AI work because a score that allocates attention or removes speech becomes a governance object, not merely a prediction. The connection to certificate transparency is important: web security already learned that private assurances become stronger when critical claims are placed in a tamper-evident public record.
ww: The mechanism should improve on policy-only transparency because it changes what must be trusted. A report asks outsiders to believe that the platform's internal records are complete and stable. An append-only log makes rewriting the past visible if the log structure and auditors behave as intended. Signed model metadata reduces ambiguity about which model version a receipt is claiming. Provenance anchoring gives later checks a fixed reference point for data and model lineage claims, so the platform cannot easily swap the story after criticism. Privacy-preserving inference receipts address the reason full public logging would fail: most requests contain information that should not be exposed. The receipt keeps the audit signal while controlling the sensitive details. Decentralised audit sampling matters because no single auditor can watch every request, and no single platform-controlled checker is enough for public trust. The reported microsecond-scale receipt cost supports the deployment argument: if the per-request overhead is very small, the protocol has a plausible path into ranking, recommendation, advertising, and moderation services that operate continuously.
po: The payoff is a deployable protocol suite for making AI-mediated web platforms more externally checkable. The paper contributes provenance anchoring, a model lineage registry, inference transparency, decentralised audit sampling, a formal threat model, and a reproducible evaluation protocol. Its measurements are deliberately limited to executable parts without proprietary dependencies: cryptographic and logging overheads plus proof verification costs. Within that scope, the abstract reports microsecond-scale receipt generation and proof sizes that grow logarithmically, which supports the claim that transparency receipts need not be too expensive for web use. The practical capability is not perfect openness; it is verifiable accountability with controlled disclosure.
limits: The abstract is careful about what is measured. It does not claim a full live deployment inside a major platform, nor does it measure ranking quality, moderation fairness, advertising outcomes, or user trust after adoption. The reported overheads cover cryptographic and logging costs, not the organizational cost of governance, standards adoption, key management, dispute resolution, or regulator access. The system assumes provenance claims and signed metadata are created honestly enough to be meaningful; anchoring a false claim only proves that the false claim existed. Privacy-preserving receipts must also be designed so they do not leak through side channels or omit facts auditors need. Audit sampling can deter cheating, but sampling is not the same as checking every inference.
